short: the fraction of a table's rows a condition matches. few rows favour an index, most rows a seq scan.
the leading columns of a multicolumn index. an index on (a, b) narrows scans on a, or on a and b.
postgres 18: using an index on (a, b) for a condition on b alone, with one search per value of a.
the EXPLAIN ANALYZE line (postgres 18+) counting how many times an index scan went down the tree.
a scan answered from the index alone, for pages the visibility map marks all-visible.
a trip from an index-only scan to the table, for a page not marked all-visible. EXPLAIN counts them as Heap Fetches.
an index that holds every column a query needs, so the query can be an index-only scan.
an index with a WHERE clause: it holds only the rows that match it.
an index on a computed value like lower(email). the query has to use the same expression.
paging by remembering the last row seen: WHERE (a, id) > (last_a, last_id), instead of OFFSET.
(a, b) > (x, y): compared column by column, like words in a dictionary. matches an index on (a, b).
one logical write turning into many physical ones: the row, an entry per index, and WAL for each.
an index type: btree, hash, GiST, SP-GiST, GIN or BRIN. listed in pg_am.
which operators an index type can serve for a data type, like gin jsonb_path_ops or btree text_pattern_ops.
text as a sorted list of normalized words (lexemes) with their positions, for full-text search.
a full-text search condition over lexemes, with & | ! and <->, matched against a tsvector with @@.
a run of three characters. pg_trgm compares and indexes text by trigrams, for LIKE '%foo%' and similarity.
